hints: A deflection greater than 90° requires a strong interaction with a concentrated region of the atom.
Recall the charge of an alpha particle and what charge is needed to repel it.
Use the rarity of these large deflections to infer where most atomic mass is located.
walkthrough: An alpha particle deflected through more than 90° has experienced a very strong repulsive interaction.
Since alpha particles are positively charged, the repelling nucleus is charged positively.
Only a small, concentrated region can cause these rare large deflections, so most of the atom's mass is concentrated in the nucleus.

ai_rubric.observable: States that the nucleus is charged.
States that the majority of the atom's mass is in the nucleus.

hints: A fundamental particle has no smaller constituent particles.
Recall the internal structure of a proton.
Use that structure to decide whether the proton is fundamental.
walkthrough: A proton is made up of quarks.
A proton is not a fundamental particle.

ai_rubric.observable: States that a proton is not fundamental because it is made up of quarks.

hints: Convert the 1.0 minute interval into seconds before using Q = It.
Each alpha particle has charge magnitude 2e, not e.
Divide the total beam charge by the charge of one alpha particle.
walkthrough: The time is 1.0 min = 60 s, so Q = It = (6.9 × 10⁻⁹ A)(60 s) = 4.14 × 10⁻⁷ C.
Each alpha particle has charge magnitude 2e = 2(1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C) = 3.20 × 10⁻¹⁹ C.
The number of alpha particles is N = Q / (2e) = (4.14 × 10⁻⁷) / (3.20 × 10⁻¹⁹) = 1.29 × 10¹².
To two significant figures, 1.3 × 10¹² alpha particles pass the point.

ai_rubric.observable: Uses Q = It with 60 s to calculate the total charge transferred.
Divides the total charge by 2e, using the charge magnitude of one alpha particle.

hints: The field strength is the same at every point in a uniform electric field.
The alpha particle's charge and mass do not change during its motion.
Link the electric force to the acceleration using Newton's second law.
walkthrough: The electric force magnitude is F = |q|E.
Both |q| and E are constant, so the electric force magnitude is constant.
For the alpha particle's constant mass, F = ma means that the acceleration magnitude is constant.

ai_rubric.observable: States that the electric force magnitude on the alpha particle is constant.
States that the acceleration magnitude is constant.

hints: Isotopes of the same element have the same number of protons, though their neutron numbers can differ.
Use the number of protons to compare the nuclear charges.
In a common electric field, compare force using F = |q|E.
walkthrough: Nuclei X and Y are isotopes, so they have the same number of protons.
They therefore have the same positive nuclear charge magnitude.
Both are in the same electric field, and F = |q|E.
Therefore the electric force magnitude on X is the same as that on Y.

ai_rubric.observable: States that the isotopes have the same charge or the same number of protons.
Concludes that the electric force magnitude is the same on both nuclei.
